Neonates of Phymaturus patagonicus emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs following a substantial incubation period, with a snout-vent length at birth of approximately 3 cm [Lb = approximately 3 cm]. This modest size at hatching is typical of many liolaemid lizards adapted to high-altitude environments, where extended embryogenesis within the cleidoic egg allows for the development of a relatively advanced yolk-sac larva. The lecithotrophic hatchling relies initially on its internalized yolk reserves before commencing exogenous feeding, a trophic switch that marks the onset of the juvenile phase. Growth during the first few months appears to be strongly temperature-dependent; under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the time elapsed from birth to the attainment of puberty has been recorded as 4 years after birth [tp = 4 years after birth], a relatively protracted juvenile period that reflects the species' slow life-history tactic. This extended pre-reproductive interval is consistent with observations in other montane Phymaturus, in which delayed maturation is thought to be an adaptation to short and unpredictable activity seasons at high elevations.

Sexual maturation in this species involves a notable divergence in body size thresholds between the sexes. Females achieve reproductive maturity upon reaching a snout-vent length of 8.5 cm [Lp = 8.5 cm], whereas males require a slightly larger body size of 8.7 cm [Lp = 8.7 cm] before puberty is initiated. This slight dimorphism in maturation size may reflect divergent selective pressures acting on each sex, with females needing to attain a minimum body volume adequate for vitellogenesis and egg retention, while males likely require a competitive body size to secure access to mates in their rocky outcrop habitats. The ages at which these thresholds are crossed are approximately equivalent under common garden conditions; field-caught individuals at a site in Neuquén Province showed that females reached puberty near 4 years after birth [tp = 4 years after birth], while males also attained puberty at approximately 4 years after birth [tp = approximately 4 years after birth], both documented at 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. Following the pubertal transition, both sexes enter the reproductively active adult phase, though growth continues at a diminished rate throughout their lives.

Females of Phymaturus patagonicus exhibit a maximum adult snout-vent length of 11 cm [Li = 11 cm], a value that is approached asymptotically after several years of post-pubertal growth. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females has been estimated at 46.8 grams [Wwi = 46.8 grams], a body mass that aligns with predictions from length-mass allometries derived for related iguanian lizards. Attaining this asymptotic size requires sustained foraging success over multiple active seasons, and field records suggest that only a fraction of individuals in a given cohort survive to reach the largest body sizes. The slow growth trajectory and modest terminal dimensions of this species are indicative of a low-resource, high-survival life-history strategy typical of many viviparous reptiles inhabiting Patagonian steppes. In comparative terms, the 46.8 gram [Wwi = 46.8 gram] mass of adult females is modest relative to that of some larger-bodied liolaemids, yet it represents a substantial energetic investment given the cold, productive-poor environments these lizards occupy.

Under stable thermal conditions at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], reproductive output in Phymaturus patagonicus is constrained by a combination of low fecundity and infrequent breeding events. Gravid females produce clutches of 2 young per reproductive event [N_R_i = 2 young per reproductive event], and available data indicate that a given female typically produces 1 clutch every 2 years [F_R_i = 1 clutch every 2 years]. This exceptionally slow reproductive rate, equivalent to approximately 0.5 offspring per female per year, is among the lowest recorded for any liolaemid lizard and underscores the energetic challenges of viviparous reproduction in a cold climate. The lengthy interval between successive clutches likely reflects the time required for a female to accumulate sufficient energy reserves following parturition, as well as the extended gestation period characteristic of this genus. Brood sizes do not appear to vary markedly with female body size within the species, suggesting that the 2 young per clutch figure [N_R_i = 2 young per clutch figure] may represent an evolutionary fixed point rather than a plastic trait.
